{{Not to be confused with|Rokhlin's theorem}}

In mathematics, the '''Rokhlin lemma''', or '''Kakutani–Rokhlin lemma''' is an important result in [[ergodic theory]]. It states that an aperiodic [[measure preserving dynamical system]] can be decomposed to an arbitrary high tower of measurable sets and a remainder of arbitrarily small measure. It was proven by [[Vladimir Abramovich Rokhlin]] and independently by [[Shizuo Kakutani]]. The lemma is used extensively in ergodic theory, for example in [[Ornstein isomorphism theorem|Ornstein theory]] and has many generalizations.

Rokhlin lemma belongs to the group mathematical statements such as [[Zorn's lemma]] in set theory and [[Schwarz lemma]] in [[complex analysis]] which are traditionally called lemmas despite the fact that their roles in their respective fields are fundamental.

==Terminology==

A '''[[Standard probability space|Lebesgue space]]''' is a measure space <math>(X, \mathcal B, \mu)</math> composed of two parts. One atomic part with finite/countably many atoms, and one continuum part isomorphic to an interval on <math display="inline">\R</math>.

We consider only '''measure-preserving maps'''. As typical in measure theory, we can freely discard countably many sets of measure zero.

An '''ergodic map''' is a map <math>T</math> such that if <math>T^{-1}(A) = A</math> (except on a measure-zero set) then <math>A</math> or <math>X-A</math> has measure zero.

An '''aperiodic map''' is a map such that the set of periodic points is measure zero:<math display="block">
\mu( \cup_{n \geq 1}\{x = T^n x\}) = 0
      </math>A '''Rokhlin tower''' is a family of sets <math display="inline">S, TS, \dots, T^{N-1}S</math> that are disjoint. <math display="inline">S</math> is called the '''base''' of the tower, and each <math display="inline">T^nS</math> is a '''rung''' or '''level''' of the tower. <math display="inline">N</math> is the '''height''' of the tower. The tower itself is <math>R := (S \cup TS \cup \dots \cup T^{N-1}S)</math>. The set outside the tower <math display="inline">X - R</math> is the '''error set'''.

There are several '''Rokhlin lemmas'''. Each states that, under some assumptions, we can construct Rokhlin towers that are arbitrarily high with arbitrarily small error sets.

{{Math theorem
| name = (ergodic)

| math_statement = If <math display="inline">T</math> is ergodic, and the space contains sets of arbitrarily small sizes, then we can construct Rokhlin towers.
}}

{{Math theorem
| name = (aperiodic)
| note = 
| math_statement = If <math display="inline">T</math> is aperiodic, and the space is Lebesgue, and has measure 1, then we can construct Rokhlin towers.
}}

{{Math theorem
| name = (aperiodic, invertible, independent base)
| note = 
| math_statement = Assume that <math display="inline">T</math> is aperiodic and invertible, and the space is Lebesgue, and has measure 1.

Given any partition of <math display="inline">X</math> into finitely many events <math display="inline">P := \{P_0, P_1, \dots, P_{K-1}\}</math>, we can construct Rokhlin towers where each level is probabilistically independent of the partition.
}}

== Applications ==
The Rokhlin lemma can be used to prove some theorems. For example, (Section 2.5 <ref name=":0" />)

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Given a dynamical system on a Lebesgue space of measure 1, where <math display="inline">T</math> is invertible and measure preserving, it is isomorphic to a stationary process on a countable alphabet.
| name = Countable generator theorem
| note = Rokhlin 1965
}}

(Section 4.6 <ref name=":0" />)

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Given a dynamical system on a Lebesgue space of measure 1, where <math display="inline">T</math> is invertible, measure preserving, and ergodic.

If its entropy is less than <math>\ln k</math>, then the system is generated by a partition into <math>k</math> subsets.
| name = Krieger finite generator theorem
| note = Krieger 1970
}}

[[Ornstein isomorphism theorem]] (Chapter 6 <ref name=":0" />).

==Topological Rokhlin lemmas ==

Let <math>\textstyle (X,T)</math> be a [[topological dynamical system]] consisting of a compact metric space <math>\textstyle X</math> and a [[homeomorphism]] <math>\textstyle T:X\rightarrow X</math>. The topological dynamical system <math>\textstyle (X,T)</math> is called '''minimal''' if it has no proper non-empty closed <math>\textstyle T</math>-invariant subsets.  It is called (topologically) '''aperiodic''' if  it has no periodic points (<math>T^{k}x=x</math> for some <math>x\in X</math> and <math>k\in\mathbb{{Z}}</math> implies <math>k=0</math>). A topological dynamical system <math>\textstyle (Y,S)</math> is called a '''factor''' of <math>\textstyle (X,T)</math> if there exists a continuous surjective mapping <math>\textstyle \varphi:X\rightarrow Y</math> which is '''equivariant''', i.e., <math>\textstyle \varphi(Tx)=S\varphi(x)</math> for all <math>\textstyle x\in X</math>.

[[Elon Lindenstrauss]] proved the following theorem:<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Mean dimension, small entropy factors and an embedding theorem|journal = [[Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS]]|date = 1999-12-01|issn = 0073-8301|pages = 227–262|volume = 89|issue = 1|doi = 10.1007/BF02698858|first = Elon|last = Lindenstrauss|s2cid = 2413058|author-link=Elon Lindenstrauss|url = http://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1999__89__227_0/}}</ref>

'''Theorem:''' Let <math>\textstyle (X,T)</math> be a topological dynamical system which has an aperiodic minimal factor. Then for integer <math>\textstyle n\in\N</math> there is a continuous function <math>\textstyle f\colon X\rightarrow\R</math> such that the set <math>\textstyle E=\{x\in X\mid f(Tx)\neq f(x)+1\}</math> satisfies <math>\textstyle E,TE,\ldots,T^{n-1}E</math> are pairwise disjoint.

Gutman proved the following theorem:<ref>Gutman, Yonatan. "Embedding ℤk-actions in cubical shifts and ℤk-symbolic extensions." [[Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems]] 31.2 (2011): 383-403.</ref>

'''Theorem:''' Let <math>(X,T)</math> be a topological dynamical system which has an aperiodic factor with the [[small boundary property]]. Then for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math>, there exists a continuous function <math>f\colon X\rightarrow\R</math> such that the set <math>\textstyle E=\{x\in X \mid f(Tx)\neq f(x)+1\}</math> satisfies <math>\operatorname{ocap}(\textstyle E)<\varepsilon</math>, where <math>\operatorname{ocap}</math> denotes [[orbit capacity]].

==Other generalizations ==
* There are versions for non-invertible measure-preserving transformations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kornfeld |first=Isaac |year=2004 |title=Some old and new Rokhlin towers |journal=Contemporary Mathematics |volume=356 |pages=145–169 |doi=10.1090/conm/356/06502 |isbn=9780821833131}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Avila |first1=Artur |author1-link=Artur Avila |last2=Candela |first2=Pablo |date=2016 |title=Towers for commuting endomorphisms, and combinatorial applications |journal=Annales de l'Institut Fourier |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=1529–1544 |arxiv=1507.07010 |doi=10.5802/aif.3042 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* [[Donald Samuel Ornstein|Donald Ornstein]] and [[Benjamin Weiss]] proved a version for free actions by countable discrete [[Amenable group|amenable]] groups.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ornstein |first1=Donald S. |author-link1=Donald Samuel Ornstein |last2=Weiss |first2=Benjamin |author-link2=Benjamin Weiss |date=1987-12-01 |title=Entropy and isomorphism theorems for actions of amenable groups |journal=[[Journal d'Analyse Mathématique]] |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=1–141 |doi=10.1007/BF02790325 |issn=0021-7670 |s2cid=120653036 |doi-access=}}</ref> 
* Carl Linderholm proved a version for periodic non-singular transformations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ionescu Tulcea |first=Alexandra |author-link=Alexandra Bellow |date=1965-01-01 |title=On the Category of Certain Classes of Transformations in Ergodic Theory |journal=[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=114 |issue=1 |pages=261–279 |doi=10.2307/1994001 |jstor=1994001}}</ref>

== Proofs ==
Proofs taken from.<ref name=":0" />

=== Useful results ===
'''Proposition.''' An ergodic map on an atomless Lebesgue space is aperiodic.

'''Proof.''' If the map is not aperiodic, then there exists a number <math display="inline">n</math>, such that the set of periodic points of period <math display="inline">n</math> has positive measure. Call the set <math display="inline">S</math>. Since measure is preserved, points outside of <math display="inline">S</math> do not map into it, nor the other way. Since the space is atomless, we can divide <math display="inline">S</math> into two halves, and <math display="inline">T</math> maps each into itself, so <math display="inline">T</math> is not ergodic.

'''Proposition.''' If there is an aperiodic map on a Lebesgue space of measure 1, then the space is atomless.

'''Proof.''' If there are atoms, then by measure-preservation, each atom can only map into another atom of greater or equal measure. If it maps into an atom of greater measure, it would drain out measure from the lighter atoms, so each atom maps to another atom of equal measure. Since the space has finite total measure, there are only finitely many atoms of a certain measure, and they must cycle back to the start eventually.

'''Proposition.''' If <math display="inline">T</math> is ergodic, then any set <math display="inline">A > 0</math> satisfies (up to a [[null set]])<math display="block">X = \cup_{k \geq 0} T^k A = \cup_{k \leq 0} T^k A</math>'''Proof.''' <math display="inline">T^{-1}(\cup_{k \leq 0} T^k A)</math> is a subset of <math display="inline">\cup_{k \leq 0} T^k A</math>, so by measure-preservation they are equal. Thus <math display="inline">\cup_{k \leq 0} T^k A</math> is a factor of <math display="inline">T</math>, and since it contains <math display="inline">A> 0</math>, it is all of <math display="inline">X</math>.

Similarly, <math display="inline">T(\cup_{k \leq 0} T^k A)</math> is a subset of <math display="inline">\cup_{k \leq 0} T^k A</math>, so by measure-preservation they are equal, etc.

=== Ergodic case ===

Let <math display="inline">A</math> be a set of measure <math display="inline">< \epsilon</math>. Since <math display="inline">T</math> is ergodic, <math display="inline">X = \cup_{k \leq 0} T^k A</math>, almost any point sooner or later falls into <math display="inline">A</math>. So we define a “time till arrival” function: <math display="block"> f(x) := \min\{n \geq 0: T^n x \in A\}
              </math> with <math display="inline">f(x) := +\infty</math> if <math display="inline">x</math> never falls into <math display="inline">A</math>. The set of <math display="inline">\{f(x) = +\infty\}</math> is null.

Now let <math display="inline">S = \{x: f(x) \in \{N, 2N, 3N, \dots\}\}</math>.

=== Aperiodic case ===

==== Simplify ====
By a previous proposition, <math>X</math> is atomless, so we can map it to the unit interval <math display="inline">(0, 1)</math>.

If we can pick a near-zero set with near-full coverage, namely some <math display="inline">A = O(\epsilon)</math> such that <math display="inline">X - \cup_{k \in \Z} T^k A = O(\epsilon)</math>, then there exists some <math display="inline">n</math>, such that <math display="inline">X - \cup_{k \leq n} T^k A = O(\epsilon)</math>, and since <math>T^{-i}(T^n A) \supset T^{n-i}A </math> for each <math>i = 0, 1, 2, \dots</math>, we have<math display="block">X - \cup_{k \leq 0} T^k (T^nA) =  O(\epsilon)</math>Now, repeating the previous construction with <math>T^n A</math>, we obtain a Rokhlin tower of height <math display="inline">N</math> and coverage <math display="inline">1-O(\epsilon)</math>.

Thus, our task reduces to picking a near-zero set with near-full coverage.

==== Constructing ''A'' ====
Pick <math display="inline">M > 1/\epsilon</math>. Let <math display="inline">S</math> be the family of sets <math display="inline">A</math> such that <math display="inline">A, T^{-1}A, \dots, T^{-M}A</math> are disjoint. Since <math display="inline">T</math> preserves measure, any <math display="inline">A \in S</math> has size <math display="inline">< \epsilon</math>.

The set <math display="inline">S</math> nonempty, because <math display="inline">\emptyset \in S</math>. It is preordered by <math display="inline">A < B</math> iff <math display="inline">\mu(B-A) = 0</math>. Any totally ordered chain contains an upper bound. So by a simple [[Zorn's lemma|Zorn-lemma]]–like argument, there exists a maximal element <math display="inline">A</math> in it. This is the desired set.

We prove by contradiction that <math display="inline">X = \cup_{k\in \Z}T^k A</math>. Assume not, then we will construct a set <math display="inline">I\cap E > 0</math>, disjoint from <math display="inline">A</math>, such that <math display="inline">A \cup (I \cap E) \in S</math>, which makes <math display="inline">A</math> no longer a maximal element, a contradiction.

==== Constructing ''E'' ====

Since we assumed <math display="inline">X - \cup_{k\in \Z}T^k A= \epsilon' > 0</math>, with positive probability, <math>
                  x \not\in \cup_{k\in \Z}T^k A</math>.

Since <math display="inline">T</math> is aperiodic, with probability 1,<math display="block">
                  (x \neq Tx) \wedge(x \neq T^2x) \wedge \dots \wedge (x \neq T^Mx) 
                  </math>And so, for a small enough <math display="inline">\delta</math>, with probability <math display="inline">> 1- \epsilon'/2</math>,<math display="block">
                  (|x - Tx| > \delta) \wedge(|x - T^2 x| > \delta) \wedge \dots \wedge (|x - T^M x| > \delta) 
                  </math>And so, for a small enough <math display="inline">\delta</math>, with probability <math display="inline">> \epsilon'/2</math>, these two events occur simultaneously. Let the event be <math display="inline">E</math>.

{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Proof that ''E'' works}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= 
Since <math display="inline">\mu(E) > 0</math>, there exists an interval <math display="inline">I</math> of length <math display="inline">< \delta</math> such that <math display="inline">\mu(E \cap I) > 0</math>.

By construction, <math display="inline">E</math> is disjoint from <math display="inline">A</math>. It remains to check that the <math display="inline">0:M</math> preimages of <math display="inline">A \cup (I \cap E)</math> are disjoint.

By construction, <math display="inline">E</math> is disjoint from <math display="inline">\cup_{k\in \Z}T^k A</math>, so the preimages of <math display="inline">A</math> are disjoint from the preimages of <math display="inline">E\cap I</math>.

Since <math display="inline">A \in S</math>, the <math display="inline">0:M</math> preimages of <math display="inline">A</math> are disjoint.

If the <math display="inline">0:M</math> preimages of <math display="inline">E\cap I</math> are not disjoint, then there exists <math display="inline">0 \leq a < b \leq M, x \in X</math>, such that <math display="inline">T^a x, T^b x \in I \cap E</math>. In other words, there exists <math display="inline">0 \leq c \leq M, x \in X</math>, such that <math display="inline">x, T^c x \in I \cap E</math>.

However, by construction, <math display="inline">x \in E</math> implies <math display="inline">T^c x</math> is repelled by <math display="inline">x</math> to at least <math display="inline">\delta</math> distance away, so <math display="inline">T^c x \not \in I</math>, contradiction.}}{{hidden end}}

=== Invertible case ===

==== Simplify ====
It suffices to prove the case where only the base of the tower is probabilistically independent of the partition. Once that case is proved, we can apply the base case to the partition <math display="inline">P \vee T^{-1} P \vee \dots \vee T^{-N+1}P</math>.

Since events with zero probability can be ignored, we only consider partitions where each event <math display="inline">P_k</math> has positive probability.

The goal is to construct a Rokhlin tower <math display="inline">R'</math> with base <math display="inline">S'</math>, such that <math>\mu(S' \cap P_i ) =\frac{1-\epsilon}{N} \mu(P_i)</math> for each <math display="inline">i \in 0:K-1</math>.

==== [[Symbolic dynamics]] ====
Given a partition <math display="inline">P</math> and a map <math display="inline">T</math>, we can trace out the orbit of every point <math display="inline">x</math> as a string of symbols <math display="inline">a_0(x), a_1(x), a_2(x), \dots</math>, such that each <math display="inline">T^i x \in P_{a_i(x)}</math>. That is, we follow <math display="inline">x</math> to <math display="inline">T^ix</math>, then check which partition it has ended up in, and write that partition’s '''name''' as <math display="inline">a_i(x)</math>.

Given any Rokhlin tower of height <math display="inline">N</math>, we can take its base <math display="inline">S</math>, and divide it into <math display="inline">K^N</math> '''equivalence classes'''. The equivalence is defined thus: two elements are equivalent iff their names have the same first-<math display="inline">N</math> symbols.

Let <math display="inline">E \subset S</math> be one such [[equivalence class]], then we call <math display="inline">E, TE, \dots, T^{N-1}E</math> a '''column''' of the Rokhlin tower.

For each word <math display="inline">a_{0:N-1}\in (0:K-1)^N</math>, let the corresponding equivalence class be <math display="inline">E_{a}</math>.

Since <math display="inline">T</math> is invertible, the columns partition the tower. One can imagine the tower made of [[string cheese]], cut up the base of the tower into the <math display="inline">K^N</math> equivalence classes, then pull it apart into <math display="inline">K^N</math> columns.

==== First Rokhlin tower ''R'' ====
Let <math display="inline">\delta \ll \epsilon</math> be very small, and let <math display="inline">M \gg N</math> be very large. Construct a Rokhlin tower with <math display="inline">M</math> levels and error set of size <math display="inline">\delta</math>. Let its base be <math display="inline">S</math>. The tower <math display="inline">R = S\cup TS \cup\dots\cup T^{M-1}S</math> has mass <math display="inline">1-\delta</math>.

Divide its base into <math display="inline">K^N</math> equivalence classes, as previously described. This divides it into <math display="inline">K^N</math> columns <math display="inline">\{E_a\}_{a}</math> where <math display="inline">a</math> ranges over the possible words <math display="inline">(0:K-1)^N</math>.

Because of how we defined the equivalence classes, each level in each column <math display="inline">T^nE_a</math> falls entirely within one of the partitions <math display="inline">P_0, \dots, P_{K-1}</math>. Therefore, the column levels <math display="inline">\{T^nE_a\}_{a, n}</math> ''almost'' make up a refinement of the partition <math display="inline">P</math>, except for an error set of size <math display="inline">\delta</math>.

That is,<math display="block">\mu(R\cap P_i) = \sum_{a \in (0:K-1)^N,\; n \in 0:M-1}\mu(T^nE_a) = \mu(P_i) + O(\delta)</math>The critical idea: If we partition each <math display="inline">T^nE_a</math> equally into <math display="inline">N</math> parts, and put one into a new Rokhlin tower base <math display="inline">S'</math>, we will have<math display="block">\mu(S'\cap P_i) = \frac{1}{N}\mu(P_i) + O(\delta)</math>

==== Second Rokhlin tower ''R''' ====
Now we construct a new base <math display="inline">S'</math> as follows: For each column based on <math display="inline">E_a</math>, add to <math display="inline">S'</math>, in a staircase pattern, the sets<math display="block">E_{a, 0}, TE_{a, 1}, \dots, T^{N-1}E_{a, N-1}</math>then wrap back to the start:
<math display="block">T^NE_{a, 0}, T^{N+1}E_{a, 1}, \dots, T^{2N-1}E_{a, N-1}</math>and so on, until the column is exhausted.
The new Rokhlin tower base <math display="inline">S'</math> is almost correct, but needs to be trimmed slightly into another set <math>S''</math>, which would satisfy <math>\mu(S''\cap P_i)  = \frac{1-\epsilon}{N}\mu(P_i)</math> for each <math display="inline">i \in 0:K-1</math>, finishing the construction. (Only now do we use the assumption that there are only finitely many partitions. If there are countably many partitions, then the trimming cannot be done.)

{{hidden begin|style=width:100%|ta1=center|border=1px #aaa solid|title=Trimming the new Rokhlin tower base}}
The new Rokhlin tower <math display="inline">S', TS', \dots, T^{N-1}S'</math>, contains almost as much mass as the original Rokhlin tower. The only lost mass is due to a small corner on the top right and bottom left of each column, which takes up <math display="inline">\leq \frac{2N^2}{MN}</math> proportion of the whole column’s mass. If we set <math display="inline">M \gg N/\delta</math>, this lost mass is still <math display="inline">O(\delta)</math>. Thus, the new Rokhlin tower still has a very small error set.

Even after accounting for the mass lost from cutting off the column corners, we still have<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
\mu(S'\cap P_i) &= \frac{1}{N}\mu(P_i) + O(\delta) + O(\delta)  \\
&= \frac{1}{N}\mu(P_i) + O(\delta) \\
&= \frac{1}{N}\mu(P_i)\times (1 + O(N\delta/\mu(P_i)))\quad\forall i = 0, 1, \dots, K-1

\end{aligned}</math>

Since there are only finitely many partitions, we can set <math display="inline">\delta = o(\frac{\epsilon}{N\min_i \mu(P_i)})</math>, we then have<math display="block">
                  \mu(S'\cap P_i)  = \frac{1}{N}\mu(P_i)\times (1 + o(1) \epsilon)
                  </math>In other words, we have real numbers <math display="inline">c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{K-1} = o(1)</math> such that <math>
                  \mu(S'\cap P_i)  = \frac{1-c_i \epsilon}{N}\mu(P_i)
                  </math>.

Now for each column <math display="inline">i = 0, 1, \dots, K-1</math>, trim away a part of <math display="inline">S'\cap P_i</math> into <math display="inline">S''\cap P_i</math>, so that <math>\mu(S''\cap P_i)  = \frac{1-\epsilon}{N}\mu(P_i)</math>. This finishes the construction.

{{hidden end}}
